articleTitle: System aspects of planar array antennas in airborne air defence radars
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Airborne air-defence radars are required to satisfy two general operational requirements namely airborne early warning (AEW), which necessitates surveillance over 360 degrees of azimuth, and airborne intercept (AI) which requires coverage of most of the hemisphere ahead of the aircraft. Mechanically-scanned antennas can utilize either reflector or array types, but some form of array of individual radiating elements is necessary to implement electronic scanning. While array antennas can, in principle, have a curved radiating surface (usually termed conformal) virtually all array antennas used in radar have constrained the radiating elements to a single plane; hence the description planar array. The system considerations which apply to the choice of planar array antennas in airborne radar are examined, first for mechanically-scanned then for electronically-scanned antennas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: A flat-plate array antenna for TVRO applications is described. The antenna is both electrically performant (in terms of gain, efficiency, polarisation purity, sidelobe suppression and input return loss) and suitable for high volume production. In addition, its physical form makes it attractive for consumer applications and is environmentally acceptable. Results are presented for a prototype model which, although fabricated in aluminium, to validate the electrical performance only, has a form which was evolved with manufacture in injection moulded plastic in mind.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A low profile loop antenna for communications using NVIS
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Describes the development of an HF loop antenna which can be used to provide two way communications between mobile sites with a range up to 300 km. Traditionally mobile communications at HF are established either using groundwave, launched by 3 m vertical whips or using skywave (NVIS) launched by horizontal dipoles. NVIS propagation is very dependent on the ionisphere which changes in density throughout the time of decade, year and day. This limits the frequency band of interest to between 1.5 MHz and 12 MHz.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations for a Telepoint antenna
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: The design of an antenna for personal communication mobile services has to meet many varied criteria. Whilst performance is an obvious critical parameter, consideration is also required on aesthetic, in particular size constraints, and naturally, cost. The paper describes some of these criteria in relation to an antenna designed for such an application, namely the Telepoint Service. The antenna was to be used not as a mobile antenna, but as one for the permanently sited base stations. The objective was to create a unit which not only acted as an antenna but as an RF combiner for up to four channels. The general requirements for the antenna design are outlined, and the evolution of the design to one using microstrip antennas described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An integrated design process for slot array antennas
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Planar slot arrays are key RF components of high performance airborne radar systems. They are commonly used in fighter aircraft and increasingly in helicopters. This type of antenna is used because it can be designed to combine high gain with low sidelobes. The intrinsic potential for high gain from a resonant slot antenna can be augmented by a larger aperture being achievable in the available space within the enclosing radome than with other types of antenna. The paper firstly describes the design and analysis techniques used in this type of antenna in order to achieve these very exacting performance levels and then goes on to review the interface between manufacture and design. Finally, the use of near field measurement techniques as a design and fault diagnosis tool are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A low-profile dual band, dual polarised array antenna module
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Describes the design of a microstrip patch antenna module intended for use in X-band satellite communications as a building-block for a variety of two-dimensional array antennas. The module can operate in duplex mode in dual orthogonal circularly polarised transmit/receive bands. The total bandwidth is about 15%. The antenna consists of a microstrip layer containing four circularly polarised patches, each with two orthogonal feed points, and a triplate layer containing a dual feed network and separate transmit/receive connectors. The patches are excited via pins connecting the two layers. The principles of sequential rotation are employed to achieve the broadband performance. The whole structure is bonded together as a sealed unit and is suitable for mass production.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Design approaches for realising an octave band, +or-60 degrees angle scanning, polarisation diverse phased array with high polarisation purity are investigated. The realisation of such an array as a low profile flat plate structure is also a requirement. Straightforward approaches using loaded waveguide elements such as dielectric filled circular or square waveguides or quad ridged structures, even with ridges protruding from the waveguide, exhibit unacceptable limitations in terms of: wideband impedance matching, realised element beamwidth and polarisation purity degradation associated with unequal E and H-plane mutual coupling. A unique approach using square evanescent mode waveguide cavities excited by printed probes near the aperture, augmented by aperture irises and a WAIM (wide angle impedance matching) sheet (high-K thin dielectric) spaced approximately lambda omicron /8 from the aperture, potentially can overcome the limitations cited above.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Describes the design of a low-profile antenna which is used to receive signals from NAVSTAR Global Positioning System satellites to enable a receiver on board an aircraft to calculate its position to high accuracies. The basic requirements of the NAVSTAR system are that the antenna be right-hand circularly polarised and dual frequency (1228 MHz and 1575 MHz) with a 20 MHz bandwidth at each. In addition the antenna must receive signals simultaneously from a number of satellites at elevation angles greater than 5 degrees above the horizon. The antenna installation under consideration is a single unit externally flush-mounted on top of the fuselage of the aircraft with the thickness of the antenna being minimised to keep aerodynamic drag low.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Prospects for varactor scanning microstrip arrays
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Flat Plate and Low Profile Mobile Antennas
abstract: Research today is directed towards the evolution of highly sophisticated phased arrays but there is also considerable interest in the development of simpler techniques offering limited beam scanning facilities but possibly lower costs along with other advantages. A novel approach is described which relies on the varactor diode control of the element excitation in a microstrip antenna. A microstrip line is designed to serve the dual role of phase shifter and feeder for microstrip arrays using the travelling-wave array principal. Recent results are summarised and the prospects of applying this new technique at higher microwave frequencies and millimetre bands, possibly using integrated antennas, is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
